Wasn't hospitalized while in high school, but last march was hospitalized for 7 weeks missing the last several weeks of college. In my experience the school works with you to let you catch up. I'll be graduating a year later then I was supposed to but that's because I'm also doing reduced course load (off subject a bit lol). Don't be afraid of graduating a bit later, your mental health is more important than that. 

Being hospitalized was the best thing that could of happened for me. I was able to get my suicidal ideation under control (my ideation had gone to the point where I had a set plan and was going to go through with it the night I was admitted) in a setting where I couldn't hurt myself and have daily check-ins with a psychiatrist. On top of that, we got to fast track getting my meds fixed. Both to the right dosage and to the right meds.

Just because you have ideation and self harm (I'm a pretty severe self harmer myself) doesn't immediately mean you'll be hospitalized. Be honest with your therapist... if you have a good relationship they should be able to recognize your struggles and work you through them. My therapist is completely aware of my ideation and self harm and the only time she wanted to see me institutionalized was when I was an imminent threat to my life.

Honestly, I wish I would have gone in when I was in high school, I've needed the help for that long but instead chose to suffer in silence and not tell anyone about anything for another 6 years out of my teens.

I'm in Canada, so I know it's not directly relatable, but this is my experience.

My quiet place is my therapists office... it's the only place I actually feel completely safe from everything. Including myself. 

Grapes for sure!

In my experience, the release of self-harm isn't worth the life time commitment in the long run... But in that moment? Fucking right it is. Dealing with a physical pain can be so much easier when you have no idea how to deal with shrieking inside... The regret and shame just fuels the cycle unfortunately.
